Dear Waveform colleagues,

In addition to what we discussed in the offline, ZTE new data provided last night has transparent FDSS-ST to non-transparent FDSS-ST comparison, so it is not any more correct to state that there is no data for that case. So I am re-adding the paragraph on FDSS-ST with ZTE numbers and stating that these are from one source. See below.

That said, I am somewhat unsure if the FDSS-SE and FDSS-ST transparent/non-transparent observations are really necessay as they are based on quite a small set of data points and the message on the transparent/non-transparent with plain FDSS is probably already relatively clear. Maybe more interesting is to acknowledge that the transparency/non-transparency is a property of base station receiver implementation choice of whether or not it is utilizing the knowledge of the Tx filter or not.

I will upload the summary with a Tdoc number shortly.



When the UE is using a steep-roll-off transmit filter with SE, and where the receiver processing utilizes the knowledge of the transmit filter, the additional gain from non-transparency is  [0 – 1.3] dB compared to using the same filter with SE, but not utilizing the knowledge of the filter in the receiver processing. Gain from the receiver knowing the transmit filter with FDSS-ST was not evaluated in isolation. ***


[When the UE is using a steep-roll-off transmit filter with ST, and where the receiver processing utilizes the knowledge of the transmit filter, one source reported additional gain from non-transparency is typically [0.3 – 0.92]*** dB compared to using the same filter, but not utilizing the knowledge of the filter in the receiver processing.]
***New data from Wednesday night, ZTE data sets 7-7, 7-8 and 7-9




Regards,
Karri

From: Karri Ranta-aho (Nokia) [log in to unmask]>
Sent: Monday, October 12, 2026 17:57
To: [log in to unmask] [log in to unmask]>; Karri Ranta-aho (Nokia) [log in to unmask]>
Subject: Re: [126bis-R20-6GR-Waveform]

Dear waveform colleagues,

As discussed at the end of today's online session, I attempted to create observations comparing transparent and non-transparent schemes with each other to kick-start Tuesday's offline.

As was the case with the large set of observations I provided for the meeting start, this heavily relies on AI, including AI checking if the observations are consistent with the source data. The tone that may look dismissive of the receive knowledge of the filter is also completely Claude and none due to me trying to feed bias into the observations. To the contrary, I eliminated some of the qualifying words and sentences of the outcome.

I also took note of Gokul's comment that SE is used to mean Spectral Efficiency and Spectral Extension, and replaced the former with SpEff.

Below what I have, the 1st paragraph being the overview where Claude offered some of its insights, and then the two sets of more detailed comparisons of transparent/non-transparent schemes with FDSS-SE and FDSS-ST:


Non-transparent schemes do not show a consistent advantage over the corresponding transparent schemes, and where compared directly, the additional gain from non-transparency is small. Non-transparent schemes show higher upper-end gains in some use cases, but not consistently; in some other use cases, transparent schemes reach similar or higher values (e.g. against π/2-BPSK without spectrum shaping for π/2-BPSK with FDSS-SE, and against QPSK with FDSS for QPSK with FDSS-SE). Against π/2-BPSK or QPSK with FDSS-SE: π/2-BPSK or QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides an additional gain of only -0.1 dB to 0.2 dB. Non-transparency typically adds approximately 0–0.5 dB for the results from the same source, filter and signal, and larger reported differences are generally linked to filter choice, power boosting, power-gain assumptions, individual worst-case samples or different source sets.


FDSS-SE: π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE does not show a robust advantage; against π/2-BPSK with FDSS-SE, it adds at most approximately 0.2 dB, against π/2-BPSK with FDSS, its range overlaps with that of π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-SE, and its highest values are attributable to transmitter assumptions. Against QPSK without spectrum shaping, QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE indicates an advantage mainly at low SpEff, but it is based on one or two sources and is not established under matched assumptions.

  *
Against π/2-BPSK without spectrum shaping: π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-SE provides 2.3–3.2 dB at SpEff 0.54 (single source, inner only); π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides 0.2–2.1 dB (inner) and -0.2 dB to 2.9 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.06–0.88 (two sources), decreasing with SpEff for one source; the single transparent result is therefore higher than the non-transparent inner range;
  *
Against π/2-BPSK with FDSS, with CFR applied to the reference scheme: only results for π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE were provided (0.5–1.3 dB at SpEff 0.06–0.38, single source, outer only);
  *
Against π/2-BPSK with FDSS: π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-SE (seven sources) provides mostly -1.5 dB to 1.5 dB, but spans -2.5 dB to 5.4 dB (inner) at SpEff 0.06–0.74 and -3.3 dB to 4.8 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.06–0.88; π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides 0.8–3.7 dB (inner, single source), increasing with SpEff, and -2.1 dB to 5.1 dB (outer, three sources) at SpEff 0.06–0.88; the overall ranges therefore overlap. The 5.1 dB value of π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE relies on a GMSK filter with power boosting and a single worst-case sample (-0.7 dB to 2.4 dB without power boosting);
  *
Against π/2-BPSK with FDSS-SE: π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides 0 dB at SpEff 0.23–0.38 and 0.1–0.2 dB at SpEff 0.49–0.60 (single source, outer only), i.e. the small gain occurs only at higher SpEff;
  *
Against QPSK without spectrum shaping: the gain of π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE at SpEff 0.74–0.88 is mainly due to a higher reported power gain rather than to non-transparency;
  *
Against QPSK without spectrum shaping: QPSK with transparent FDSS-SE (ten sources) provides mostly -2 dB to 1 dB at SpEff 0.06–1.33, decreasing with SpEff; QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE (two sources) provides 1.4–2.6 dB (inner, single source) and 2.2–2.9 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.06–0.60, decreasing to -0.3 dB to 2.1 dB at SpEff 0.74–1.33; the non-transparent results are therefore higher, mainly at SpEff 0.06–0.60;
  *
Against QPSK with FDSS: QPSK with transparent FDSS-SE (seven sources) provides -2.0 dB to 2.8 dB (inner) and -1.9 dB to 1.8 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.38–1.4; QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides -0.2 dB to 1.0 dB at SpEff 0.38–0.60 (single source, outer only); the non-transparent result is therefore within the transparent range;
  *
Against QPSK with FDSS, with CFR applied to the reference scheme: only results for QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE were provided (-0.15 dB to 0.9 dB at SpEff 0.38–0.60, single source, outer only);
  *
Against QPSK with FDSS-SE: QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides only -0.1 dB to 0 dB at SpEff 0.23–0.74 and 0.1–0.2 dB at SpEff 0.88–1.18 (single source, outer only);
  *
Against QPSK without spectrum shaping, with CFR applied to the reference scheme: QPSK with transparent FDSS-SE provides -2.6 dB to 0.45 dB at SpEff 0.60–1.33 (two sources); QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides -0.3 dB to 1.45 dB at SpEff 0.74–1.33 (single source, outer only); both are therefore reduced, while the non-transparent upper end remains approximately 1 dB higher.

FDSS-ST: π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-ST generally shows higher reported gains than π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-ST, in particular against QPSK without spectrum shaping; however, against π/2-BPSK with FDSS, the outer non-transparent result is largely within the transparent range, and the non-transparent results rest on few and different sources.

  *
Against QPSK without spectrum shaping: π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-ST (six sources) provides -1.5 dB to 0.2 dB (inner) and -0.8 dB to 1.4 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.74–1.33; π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-ST (two sources) provides 1.9–2.6 dB (inner) at SpEff 0.74–0.88 and 0.9–2.0 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.75–1.31; the non-transparent results are therefore higher in this SpEff range;
  *
Against π/2-BPSK with FDSS: π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-ST (eleven sources) provides mostly -1.9 dB to 1.0 dB at SpEff 0.06–0.60, and -0.1 dB to 3.3 dB (inner) and -0.7 dB to 2.0 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.74–0.88; π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-ST provides 2.2–4.6 dB (inner, single source) at SpEff 0.19–0.88 and -1.8 dB to 1.2 dB (outer, single source) at SpEff 0.06–0.74; the inner non-transparent result is therefore higher, while the outer non-transparent result is largely within the transparent range;
  *
Against π/2-BPSK without spectrum shaping: only results for π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-ST were provided (0.7–1.6 dB at SpEff 0.06–0.38, decreasing to 0.1–1.2 dB at SpEff 0.49–0.88, single source);
  *
Against QPSK with FDSS: only results for π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-ST were provided (2.2–4.0 dB at SpEff 0.06–0.74 and -1.3 dB to 1.6 dB at SpEff 1.0–1.4, two sources, inner only);
  *
Against π/2-BPSK with FDSS or QPSK without spectrum shaping, with CFR applied to the reference scheme: only results for π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-ST were provided (against π/2-BPSK with FDSS: -2.1 dB to 0.6 dB (inner) and -1.7 dB to 0 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.06–0.60, single source; against QPSK without spectrum shaping: 0–1.0 dB at SpEff 0.60–0.88 and -1.9 dB to 0.6 dB at SpEff 1.03–1.33, two sources).

Regards,
Karri
[cid:88ee6a52-4d27-4f15-805e-c2a1e1029c7f]

From: 3gpp_tsg_ran_wg1: tsg ran working group 1 [log in to unmask]> on behalf of Karri Ranta-aho (Nokia) [log in to unmask]>
Sent: Monday, October 12, 2026 11:51
To: [log in to unmask] [log in to unmask]>
Subject: Re: [126bis-R20-6GR-Waveform]

Dear Waveform Colleagues,

Thank you for the excellent discussion on the offline.


  1.
Based on what we discussed, I have lifted a handful of FDSS observations from the summary that we could try to discuss online tonight. I have two alternative branches that we could pick which one to discuss, or even consider a merge.
  2.
I have another batch of observations on impact of filter change to FDSS. I have it here "just in case", to set the stage for potentially concluding that the 5G FDSS requirements that define the constraints of the filter could be revisited. We might not have the time to go there yet.
  3.
A proposal to update the RAN1#125 agreement on FDSS to remove the FFS point on QPSK and 16QAM. This would effectively limit the transparent FDSS to pi/2 BPSK
  4.
A proposed conclusion on the definition of what non-transparent means. We don't necessarily have to agree on this definition, the important point is to identify if this is broadly assumed by the group, or if there is controversy.

I will upload the FL summary#1 with a Tdoc number shortly.




Feature lead proposal:

Discuss the following observations alternatives on FDSS

Alternative 1

Transparent FDSS compared with no spectrum shaping (use cases 1–4): For π/2-BPSK (two sources), FDSS provides a net gain of 0.8–1.6 dB (outer) and -0.3 dB to 0.9 dB (inner) at SE 0.23–0.31. For QPSK (four sources), most results are within -2.8 dB to 0.9 dB at SE 0.23–1.33, with a large spread across sources. For 16QAM (two sources), FDSS results in a net loss of 2.2–3.6 dB (inner) and 1.5–2.9 dB (outer) at SE 1.48–2.57. When CFR is applied to the reference scheme, the net gain is -0.2 dB to 0.2 dB for QPSK at SE 0.74–1.33 (single source) and -0.7 dB to 0.2 dB for 16QAM at SE 1.33–2.57 (single source, inner only).

FDSS filter change (use cases 9 and 12, π/2-BPSK, outer RB allocation only): For transparent FDSS (three sources), the net gain is 0.1–4.6 dB at SE 0.06–0.60, with two sources reporting approximately 0 dB at SE 0.24, and -0.3 dB to 3.7 dB at SE 0.74. For non-transparent FDSS (three sources), two sources report a net gain of 0.6–0.9 dB and 2.5 dB at SE 0.06–0.60, while the third source reports 0–4.9 dB at SE 0.06–0.74, depending on the filter configuration. When CFR is applied to the reference scheme (single source), the net gain of non-transparent FDSS is 0.55–0.75 dB at SE 0.06–0.60.

Alternative 2

Compared with no spectrum shaping, transparent FDSS provides a net gain for π/2-BPSK, mainly for outer RB allocation. For QPSK, most results show a moderate net loss or a small net gain, with a large spread across sources. For 16QAM, most results show a net loss. When CFR is applied to the reference scheme, the net gain of FDSS for QPSK and 16QAM is within approximately ±0.7 dB.

-   FDSS for π/2-BPSK (Use case 1), reference scheme without CFR (two sources): a net gain of -0.3 dB to 0.9 dB (inner) and 0.8–1.6 dB (outer) at SE 0.23–0.31; one source reports a net gain of 3.6 dB at SE 0.54 (inner only). No results were provided with CFR applied to the reference scheme;

-   FDSS for QPSK (Use case 2), reference scheme without CFR (four sources): most results are within a net gain of -2.8 dB to 0.9 dB at SE 0.23–1.33, and outer RB allocation generally performs better than inner; one source reports net losses of up to 12.5 dB, and one source reports a net gain of 2.0 dB at SE 1.08 (inner only). With CFR applied to the reference scheme (single source), the net gain is -0.2 dB to -0.1 dB (inner) and 0.1–0.2 dB (outer) at SE 0.74–1.33;

-   FDSS for 16QAM (use case 3), reference scheme without CFR (two sources): a net loss of 2.2–3.6 dB (inner) and 1.5–2.9 dB (outer) at SE 1.48–2.57; one source reports a net gain of 0.2 dB at SE 2.16 (inner only). With CFR applied to the reference scheme (single source, inner only), the net gain is -0.7 dB to 0.2 dB at SE 1.33–2.57;


Discuss the following observations on FDSS with different filters

Comparing FDSS with a steeper filter, results available for π/2-BPSK  and outer RB allocations only.

-   Filter change for non-transparent FDSS for π/2-BPSK (Use case 9), reference scheme without CFR (three sources): a net gain of 0–4.9 dB at SE 0.06–0.74, decreasing slightly with increasing SE; the spread is mainly due to different filter configurations within one source, while the other sources report 0.6–0.9 dB and 2.5 dB at SE 0.06–0.60. With CFR applied to the reference scheme (single source), the net gain is 0.55–0.75 dB at SE 0.06–0.60;

-   Filter change for transparent FDSS for π/2-BPSK (Use case 12), reference scheme without CFR (three sources): a net gain of 0.1–4.6 dB at SE 0.06–0.60 and of -0.3 dB to 3.7 dB at SE 0.74; two sources report a net gain of approximately 0 dB at SE 0.24. No results were provided with CFR applied to the reference scheme.


Feature lead proposal:

Update the RAN1#125 agreement as follows:

  *   FDSS with transparent filtering should be supported in 6G is beneficial to be supported for π/2-BPSK from RAN1 perspective
     *   FFS: QPSK, 16QAM
  *   Draft LS to RAN4
     *   FFS: contents e.g., “the exact filter requirements are up to RAN4 discussions.”

Feature lead proposal:

Discuss the following conclusion:

  *   RAN1 work on non-transparent FDSS/FDSS-SE/FDSS-ST focuses on techniques where the DMRS and the data signal both go through the same filter. If a non-transparent FDSS/FDSS-SE/FDSS-ST is agreed to be included in 6G, the filter would be defined by RAN1.



Regards,
Karri

snippet:
Hi all,

Following the version we had at the end of yesterday online session, the proposal has been reorganized as follows for your consideration in Section 6.1.1.3.

Proposal 1-3-2-Wed:
For dynamic adjustment of parameters at least for SPS-PDSCH configurations and CG-PUSCH configurations that are not immediately activated and are subsequently activated by an activation DCI, study which parameter is or is not dynamically adjusted. [...]
body:
Hi all,

Following the version we had at the end of yesterday online session, the proposal has been reorganized as follows for your consideration in Section 6.1.1.3.

Proposal 1-3-2-Wed:
For dynamic adjustment of parameters at least for SPS-PDSCH configurations and CG-PUSCH configurations that are not immediately activated and are subsequently activated by an activation DCI, study which parameter is or is not dynamically adjusted.

  *   Dynamic adjustment via activation DCI is considered as starting point.
  *   The parameters that could be dynamically adjusted via activation DCI for SPS-PDSCH and Type 2 CG-PUSCH in 5G NR is considered as starting point.
     *   For parameters that are configured via RRC for SPS-PDSCH and Type 2 CG-PUSCH in 5G NR, such as periodicity, study whether any of them can be dynamically adjusted in 6GR.
     *   For parameters that could be dynamically adjusted via activation DCI for SPS-PDSCH and Type 2 CG-PUSCH in 5G NR, study whether any of them cannot be dynamically adjusted in 6GR.
     *   For parameters that are indicated via activation DCI and could not be dynamically adjusted for SPS-PDSCH and Type 2 CG-PUSCH in 5G NR, study whether any of them can be dynamically adjusted in 6GR.

BR/Lei

Proposal 1-2-1 (B):

[However, such adaptation is currently realized through re-activation procedures, which may introduce signaling overhead and procedural constraints in some scenarios.]
  *   Similar benefits may also be relevant for 6GR. Given the highly dynamic traffic characteristics, channel conditions, and spatial-domain environments anticipated for emerging services such as XR and AI traffic, dynamic adjustment of CG PUSCH and SPS PDSCH parameters could improve resource utilization, transmission efficiency, and adaptability to varying conditions[, while reducing the need for frequent RRC reconfiguration or repeated re-activation procedures].
  *   Note: The text enclosed with square brackets is subject to further discussion.

body:
Dear Waveform colleagues,

In addition to what we discussed in the offline, ZTE new data provided last night has transparent FDSS-ST to non-transparent FDSS-ST comparison, so it is not any more correct to state that there is no data for that case. So I am re-adding the paragraph on FDSS-ST with ZTE numbers and stating that these are from one source. See below.

That said, I am somewhat unsure if the FDSS-SE and FDSS-ST transparent/non-transparent observations are really necessay as they are based on quite a small set of data points and the message on the transparent/non-transparent with plain FDSS is probably already relatively clear. Maybe more interesting is to acknowledge that the transparency/non-transparency is a property of base station receiver implementation choice of whether or not it is utilizing the knowledge of the Tx filter or not.

I will upload the summary with a Tdoc number shortly.



When the UE is using a steep-roll-off transmit filter with SE, and where the receiver processing utilizes the knowledge of the transmit filter, the additional gain from non-transparency is  [0 – 1.3] dB compared to using the same filter with SE, but not utilizing the knowledge of the filter in the receiver processing. Gain from the receiver knowing the transmit filter with FDSS-ST was not evaluated in isolation. ***


[When the UE is using a steep-roll-off transmit filter with ST, and where the receiver processing utilizes the knowledge of the transmit filter, one source reported additional gain from non-transparency is typically [0.3 – 0.92]*** dB compared to using the same filter, but not utilizing the knowledge of the filter in the receiver processing.]
***New data from Wednesday night, ZTE data sets 7-7, 7-8 and 7-9




Regards,
Karri

Subject: Re: [126bis-R20-6GR-Waveform]

Dear waveform colleagues,

As discussed at the end of today's online session, I attempted to create observations comparing transparent and non-transparent schemes with each other to kick-start Tuesday's offline.

As was the case with the large set of observations I provided for the meeting start, this heavily relies on AI, including AI checking if the observations are consistent with the source data. The tone that may look dismissive of the receive knowledge of the filter is also completely Claude and none due to me trying to feed bias into the observations. To the contrary, I eliminated some of the qualifying words and sentences of the outcome.

I also took note of Gokul's comment that SE is used to mean Spectral Efficiency and Spectral Extension, and replaced the former with SpEff.

Below what I have, the 1st paragraph being the overview where Claude offered some of its insights, and then the two sets of more detailed comparisons of transparent/non-transparent schemes with FDSS-SE and FDSS-ST:


Non-transparent schemes do not show a consistent advantage over the corresponding transparent schemes, and where compared directly, the additional gain from non-transparency is small. Non-transparent schemes show higher upper-end gains in some use cases, but not consistently; in some other use cases, transparent schemes reach similar or higher values (e.g. against π/2-BPSK without spectrum shaping for π/2-BPSK with FDSS-SE, and against QPSK with FDSS for QPSK with FDSS-SE). Against π/2-BPSK or QPSK with FDSS-SE: π/2-BPSK or QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides an additional gain of only -0.1 dB to 0.2 dB. Non-transparency typically adds approximately 0–0.5 dB for the results from the same source, filter and signal, and larger reported differences are generally linked to filter choice, power boosting, power-gain assumptions, individual worst-case samples or different source sets.


FDSS-SE: π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE does not show a robust advantage; against π/2-BPSK with FDSS-SE, it adds at most approximately 0.2 dB, against π/2-BPSK with FDSS, its range overlaps with that of π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-SE, and its highest values are attributable to transmitter assumptions. Against QPSK without spectrum shaping, QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE indicates an advantage mainly at low SpEff, but it is based on one or two sources and is not established under matched assumptions.

  *
Against π/2-BPSK without spectrum shaping: π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-SE provides 2.3–3.2 dB at SpEff 0.54 (single source, inner only); π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides 0.2–2.1 dB (inner) and -0.2 dB to 2.9 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.06–0.88 (two sources), decreasing with SpEff for one source; the single transparent result is therefore higher than the non-transparent inner range;
  *
Against π/2-BPSK with FDSS, with CFR applied to the reference scheme: only results for π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE were provided (0.5–1.3 dB at SpEff 0.06–0.38, single source, outer only);
  *
Against π/2-BPSK with FDSS: π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-SE (seven sources) provides mostly -1.5 dB to 1.5 dB, but spans -2.5 dB to 5.4 dB (inner) at SpEff 0.06–0.74 and -3.3 dB to 4.8 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.06–0.88; π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides 0.8–3.7 dB (inner, single source), increasing with SpEff, and -2.1 dB to 5.1 dB (outer, three sources) at SpEff 0.06–0.88; the overall ranges therefore overlap. The 5.1 dB value of π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE relies on a GMSK filter with power boosting and a single worst-case sample (-0.7 dB to 2.4 dB without power boosting);
  *
Against π/2-BPSK with FDSS-SE: π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides 0 dB at SpEff 0.23–0.38 and 0.1–0.2 dB at SpEff 0.49–0.60 (single source, outer only), i.e. the small gain occurs only at higher SpEff;
  *
Against QPSK without spectrum shaping: the gain of π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE at SpEff 0.74–0.88 is mainly due to a higher reported power gain rather than to non-transparency;
  *
Against QPSK without spectrum shaping: QPSK with transparent FDSS-SE (ten sources) provides mostly -2 dB to 1 dB at SpEff 0.06–1.33, decreasing with SpEff; QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE (two sources) provides 1.4–2.6 dB (inner, single source) and 2.2–2.9 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.06–0.60, decreasing to -0.3 dB to 2.1 dB at SpEff 0.74–1.33; the non-transparent results are therefore higher, mainly at SpEff 0.06–0.60;
  *
Against QPSK with FDSS: QPSK with transparent FDSS-SE (seven sources) provides -2.0 dB to 2.8 dB (inner) and -1.9 dB to 1.8 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.38–1.4; QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides -0.2 dB to 1.0 dB at SpEff 0.38–0.60 (single source, outer only); the non-transparent result is therefore within the transparent range;
  *
Against QPSK with FDSS, with CFR applied to the reference scheme: only results for QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE were provided (-0.15 dB to 0.9 dB at SpEff 0.38–0.60, single source, outer only);
  *
Against QPSK with FDSS-SE: QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides only -0.1 dB to 0 dB at SpEff 0.23–0.74 and 0.1–0.2 dB at SpEff 0.88–1.18 (single source, outer only);
  *
Against QPSK without spectrum shaping, with CFR applied to the reference scheme: QPSK with transparent FDSS-SE provides -2.6 dB to 0.45 dB at SpEff 0.60–1.33 (two sources); QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides -0.3 dB to 1.45 dB at SpEff 0.74–1.33 (single source, outer only); both are therefore reduced, while the non-transparent upper end remains approximately 1 dB higher.

FDSS-ST: π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-ST generally shows higher reported gains than π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-ST, in particular against QPSK without spectrum shaping; however, against π/2-BPSK with FDSS, the outer non-transparent result is largely within the transparent range, and the non-transparent results rest on few and different sources.

  *
Against QPSK without spectrum shaping: π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-ST (six sources) provides -1.5 dB to 0.2 dB (inner) and -0.8 dB to 1.4 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.74–1.33; π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-ST (two sources) provides 1.9–2.6 dB (inner) at SpEff 0.74–0.88 and 0.9–2.0 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.75–1.31; the non-transparent results are therefore higher in this SpEff range;
  *
Against π/2-BPSK with FDSS: π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-ST (eleven sources) provides mostly -1.9 dB to 1.0 dB at SpEff 0.06–0.60, and -0.1 dB to 3.3 dB (inner) and -0.7 dB to 2.0 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.74–0.88; π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-ST provides 2.2–4.6 dB (inner, single source) at SpEff 0.19–0.88 and -1.8 dB to 1.2 dB (outer, single source) at SpEff 0.06–0.74; the inner non-transparent result is therefore higher, while the outer non-transparent result is largely within the transparent range;
  *
Against π/2-BPSK without spectrum shaping: only results for π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-ST were provided (0.7–1.6 dB at SpEff 0.06–0.38, decreasing to 0.1–1.2 dB at SpEff 0.49–0.88, single source);
  *
Against QPSK with FDSS: only results for π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-ST were provided (2.2–4.0 dB at SpEff 0.06–0.74 and -1.3 dB to 1.6 dB at SpEff 1.0–1.4, two sources, inner only);
  *
Against π/2-BPSK with FDSS or QPSK without spectrum shaping, with CFR applied to the reference scheme: only results for π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-ST were provided (against π/2-BPSK with FDSS: -2.1 dB to 0.6 dB (inner) and -1.7 dB to 0 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.06–0.60, single source; against QPSK without spectrum shaping: 0–1.0 dB at SpEff 0.60–0.88 and -1.9 dB to 0.6 dB at SpEff 1.03–1.33, two sources).

Regards,
Karri
[cid:88ee6a52-4d27-4f15-805e-c2a1e1029c7f]

Dear Waveform Colleagues,

Thank you for the excellent discussion on the offline.


  1.
Based on what we discussed, I have lifted a handful of FDSS observations from the summary that we could try to discuss online tonight. I have two alternative branches that we could pick which one to discuss, or even consider a merge.
  2.
I have another batch of observations on impact of filter change to FDSS. I have it here "just in case", to set the stage for potentially concluding that the 5G FDSS requirements that define the constraints of the filter could be revisited. We might not have the time to go there yet.
  3.
A proposal to update the RAN1#125 agreement on FDSS to remove the FFS point on QPSK and 16QAM. This would effectively limit the transparent FDSS to pi/2 BPSK
  4.
A proposed conclusion on the definition of what non-transparent means. We don't necessarily have to agree on this definition, the important point is to identify if this is broadly assumed by the group, or if there is controversy.

I will upload the FL summary#1 with a Tdoc number shortly.




Feature lead proposal:

Discuss the following observations alternatives on FDSS

Alternative 1

Transparent FDSS compared with no spectrum shaping (use cases 1–4): For π/2-BPSK (two sources), FDSS provides a net gain of 0.8–1.6 dB (outer) and -0.3 dB to 0.9 dB (inner) at SE 0.23–0.31. For QPSK (four sources), most results are within -2.8 dB to 0.9 dB at SE 0.23–1.33, with a large spread across sources. For 16QAM (two sources), FDSS results in a net loss of 2.2–3.6 dB (inner) and 1.5–2.9 dB (outer) at SE 1.48–2.57. When CFR is applied to the reference scheme, the net gain is -0.2 dB to 0.2 dB for QPSK at SE 0.74–1.33 (single source) and -0.7 dB to 0.2 dB for 16QAM at SE 1.33–2.57 (single source, inner only).

FDSS filter change (use cases 9 and 12, π/2-BPSK, outer RB allocation only): For transparent FDSS (three sources), the net gain is 0.1–4.6 dB at SE 0.06–0.60, with two sources reporting approximately 0 dB at SE 0.24, and -0.3 dB to 3.7 dB at SE 0.74. For non-transparent FDSS (three sources), two sources report a net gain of 0.6–0.9 dB and 2.5 dB at SE 0.06–0.60, while the third source reports 0–4.9 dB at SE 0.06–0.74, depending on the filter configuration. When CFR is applied to the reference scheme (single source), the net gain of non-transparent FDSS is 0.55–0.75 dB at SE 0.06–0.60.

Alternative 2

Compared with no spectrum shaping, transparent FDSS provides a net gain for π/2-BPSK, mainly for outer RB allocation. For QPSK, most results show a moderate net loss or a small net gain, with a large spread across sources. For 16QAM, most results show a net loss. When CFR is applied to the reference scheme, the net gain of FDSS for QPSK and 16QAM is within approximately ±0.7 dB.

-   FDSS for π/2-BPSK (Use case 1), reference scheme without CFR (two sources): a net gain of -0.3 dB to 0.9 dB (inner) and 0.8–1.6 dB (outer) at SE 0.23–0.31; one source reports a net gain of 3.6 dB at SE 0.54 (inner only). No results were provided with CFR applied to the reference scheme;

-   FDSS for QPSK (Use case 2), reference scheme without CFR (four sources): most results are within a net gain of -2.8 dB to 0.9 dB at SE 0.23–1.33, and outer RB allocation generally performs better than inner; one source reports net losses of up to 12.5 dB, and one source reports a net gain of 2.0 dB at SE 1.08 (inner only). With CFR applied to the reference scheme (single source), the net gain is -0.2 dB to -0.1 dB (inner) and 0.1–0.2 dB (outer) at SE 0.74–1.33;

-   FDSS for 16QAM (use case 3), reference scheme without CFR (two sources): a net loss of 2.2–3.6 dB (inner) and 1.5–2.9 dB (outer) at SE 1.48–2.57; one source reports a net gain of 0.2 dB at SE 2.16 (inner only). With CFR applied to the reference scheme (single source, inner only), the net gain is -0.7 dB to 0.2 dB at SE 1.33–2.57;


Discuss the following observations on FDSS with different filters

Comparing FDSS with a steeper filter, results available for π/2-BPSK  and outer RB allocations only.

-   Filter change for non-transparent FDSS for π/2-BPSK (Use case 9), reference scheme without CFR (three sources): a net gain of 0–4.9 dB at SE 0.06–0.74, decreasing slightly with increasing SE; the spread is mainly due to different filter configurations within one source, while the other sources report 0.6–0.9 dB and 2.5 dB at SE 0.06–0.60. With CFR applied to the reference scheme (single source), the net gain is 0.55–0.75 dB at SE 0.06–0.60;

-   Filter change for transparent FDSS for π/2-BPSK (Use case 12), reference scheme without CFR (three sources): a net gain of 0.1–4.6 dB at SE 0.06–0.60 and of -0.3 dB to 3.7 dB at SE 0.74; two sources report a net gain of approximately 0 dB at SE 0.24. No results were provided with CFR applied to the reference scheme.


Feature lead proposal:

Update the RAN1#125 agreement as follows:

  *   FDSS with transparent filtering should be supported in 6G is beneficial to be supported for π/2-BPSK from RAN1 perspective
     *   FFS: QPSK, 16QAM
  *   Draft LS to RAN4
     *   FFS: contents e.g., “the exact filter requirements are up to RAN4 discussions.”

Feature lead proposal:

Discuss the following conclusion:

  *   RAN1 work on non-transparent FDSS/FDSS-SE/FDSS-ST focuses on techniques where the DMRS and the data signal both go through the same filter. If a non-transparent FDSS/FDSS-SE/FDSS-ST is agreed to be included in 6G, the filter would be defined by RAN1.



Regards,
Karri

body:
Dear Xin, all,
Thank you. We couldn’t find a place to provide feedback on Proposal 5.2.2-1r2, please find them below.
In our view, how the UE performs the RLM measurements is up to the UE and whether the UE performs the measurements in EE or non-EE mode should also be left to UE implementation (our position was not captured in Section 5.2.5 of the FL summary). We would therefore like to add the following points to Proposal 5.2.2-1r2:

  *   The achievable RLM accuracy in EE mode is highly dependent on UE implementation.
  *   The observations collected from the evaluation results may not necessarily lead to specification changes.

Besides, I’d like to check with you on whether you plan to discuss the proposals related to core wake-up functionality? The discussions have focused mostly on measurements so far and we have not discussed some of the core wake-up proposals yet.
Best Regards,
Diana
Qualcomm

Subject: Re: [126bis-R20-6GR-DL/UL transmission without dynamic scheduling]Email Discussion for AI 10.5.4.2

Dear all,

FL#1 has been uploaded as R1-2607824.

The following proposals and observations are going to be put forward in tomorrow morning’s online session.

Proposal 1-2-1 (A):
·        DCI-based dynamic activation is supported in 6GR for a SPS-PDSCH configuration.
·        DCI-based dynamic activation is at least supported in 6GR for a CG-PUSCH configuration which is not immediately activated upon the configuration.
·        FFS: Details of activation DCI for SPS-PDSCH configurations and CG-PUSCH configurations.
·        FFS: Application of activation DCI to a CG-PUSCH configuration which is immediately activated upon the configuration.
·        FFS: Potential application of sequence-based activation signaling, if a relevant need is identified.

Proposal 1-2-1 (B):
·        DCI-based dynamic activation is supported in 6GR for a SPS-PDSCH configuration.
·        DCI-based dynamic activation is at least supported in 6GR for a CG-PUSCH configuration which is not immediately activated upon the configuration.
·        FFS: Details of activation DCI for SPS-PDSCH configurations and CG-PUSCH configurations.
·        FFS: Application of activation DCI to a CG-PUSCH configuration which is immediately activated upon the configuration.
·        FFS: Potential application of sequence-based activation signaling, if a relevant need is identified.

Proposal 1-3-2: Support dynamic adjustment of parameters at least for SPS-PDSCH configurations and CG-PUSCH configurations that are not immediately activated and are subsequently activated by an activation DCI.

  *   FFS: Whether dynamic adjustment of parameters could also be applied to a CG-PUSCH configuration activated immediately upon the configuration.
     *   Note: If such support is agreed, a unified dynamic-adjustment DCI design should be pursued across all CG-PUSCH configurations and [SPS configurations].

Observation 1-3-1:

  *   NR already supports dynamic adjustment of parameters for SPS PDSCH and Type-2 CG PUSCH transmissions through activation (re-activation) DCI, demonstrating the benefits of adapting configured transmissions to varying traffic demands and channel conditions without RRC reconfiguration. [However, such adaptation is currently realized through re-activation procedures, which may introduce signaling overhead and procedural constraints in some scenarios.]
  *   Similar benefits may also be relevant for 6GR. Given the highly dynamic traffic characteristics, channel conditions, and spatial-domain environments anticipated for emerging services such as XR and AI traffic, dynamic adjustment of CG PUSCH and SPS PDSCH parameters could improve resource utilization, transmission efficiency, and adaptability to varying conditions[, while reducing the need for frequent RRC reconfiguration or repeated re-activation procedures].
  *   Note: The text enclosed with square brackets is subject to further discussion.

Proposal 2-1-1: From the RAN1 perspective, UL skipping is supported for CG-PUSCH in 6GR.

  *   For a UE configured with a CG-PUSCH configuration, the UE skips a CG-PUSCH transmission when no uplink payload is available for the CG-PUSCH.
     *   Further details are FFS.
·        Note: Further confirmation from RAN2 may be required regarding the support of UL skipping for CG-PUSCH.

Observation 2-1-2: UL skipping mechanism can enhance the efficiency of CG-PUSCH transmissions by avoiding unnecessary transmissions when no uplink data is available, leading to reduced UE power consumption and uplink interference.

Best regards,
Lei

RAN1 thanks RAN2 for the LS R2-2605860 on the R20 dynamic activation/deactivation of RRC-configured LTM measurement and reporting configurations via MAC CE. RAN1 has discussed the LS and provides the following feedback.
Applicable report types: RAN1 has no concern with applying the R20 dynamic L1 measurement and reporting configuration change to both gNB-scheduled (periodic, semi-persistent and aperiodic) and event-triggered LTM CSI reporting.

From: Karri Ranta-aho (Nokia) [log in to unmask]>
Sent: Monday, October 12, 2026 17:57
To: [log in to unmask] [log in to unmask]>; Karri Ranta-aho (Nokia) [log in to unmask]>
Subject: Re: [126bis-R20-6GR-Waveform]

Dear waveform colleagues,

As discussed at the end of today's online session, I attempted to create observations comparing transparent and non-transparent schemes with each other to kick-start Tuesday's offline.

As was the case with the large set of observations I provided for the meeting start, this heavily relies on AI, including AI checking if the observations are consistent with the source data. The tone that may look dismissive of the receive knowledge of the filter is also completely Claude and none due to me trying to feed bias into the observations. To the contrary, I eliminated some of the qualifying words and sentences of the outcome.

I also took note of Gokul's comment that SE is used to mean Spectral Efficiency and Spectral Extension, and replaced the former with SpEff.

Below what I have, the 1st paragraph being the overview where Claude offered some of its insights, and then the two sets of more detailed comparisons of transparent/non-transparent schemes with FDSS-SE and FDSS-ST:


Non-transparent schemes do not show a consistent advantage over the corresponding transparent schemes, and where compared directly, the additional gain from non-transparency is small. Non-transparent schemes show higher upper-end gains in some use cases, but not consistently; in some other use cases, transparent schemes reach similar or higher values (e.g. against π/2-BPSK without spectrum shaping for π/2-BPSK with FDSS-SE, and against QPSK with FDSS for QPSK with FDSS-SE). Against π/2-BPSK or QPSK with FDSS-SE: π/2-BPSK or QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides an additional gain of only -0.1 dB to 0.2 dB. Non-transparency typically adds approximately 0–0.5 dB for the results from the same source, filter and signal, and larger reported differences are generally linked to filter choice, power boosting, power-gain assumptions, individual worst-case samples or different source sets.


FDSS-SE: π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE does not show a robust advantage; against π/2-BPSK with FDSS-SE, it adds at most approximately 0.2 dB, against π/2-BPSK with FDSS, its range overlaps with that of π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-SE, and its highest values are attributable to transmitter assumptions. Against QPSK without spectrum shaping, QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE indicates an advantage mainly at low SpEff, but it is based on one or two sources and is not established under matched assumptions.

  *
Against π/2-BPSK without spectrum shaping: π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-SE provides 2.3–3.2 dB at SpEff 0.54 (single source, inner only); π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides 0.2–2.1 dB (inner) and -0.2 dB to 2.9 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.06–0.88 (two sources), decreasing with SpEff for one source; the single transparent result is therefore higher than the non-transparent inner range;
  *
Against π/2-BPSK with FDSS, with CFR applied to the reference scheme: only results for π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE were provided (0.5–1.3 dB at SpEff 0.06–0.38, single source, outer only);
  *
Against π/2-BPSK with FDSS: π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-SE (seven sources) provides mostly -1.5 dB to 1.5 dB, but spans -2.5 dB to 5.4 dB (inner) at SpEff 0.06–0.74 and -3.3 dB to 4.8 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.06–0.88; π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides 0.8–3.7 dB (inner, single source), increasing with SpEff, and -2.1 dB to 5.1 dB (outer, three sources) at SpEff 0.06–0.88; the overall ranges therefore overlap. The 5.1 dB value of π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE relies on a GMSK filter with power boosting and a single worst-case sample (-0.7 dB to 2.4 dB without power boosting);
  *
Against π/2-BPSK with FDSS-SE: π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides 0 dB at SpEff 0.23–0.38 and 0.1–0.2 dB at SpEff 0.49–0.60 (single source, outer only), i.e. the small gain occurs only at higher SpEff;
  *
Against QPSK without spectrum shaping: the gain of π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE at SpEff 0.74–0.88 is mainly due to a higher reported power gain rather than to non-transparency;
  *
Against QPSK without spectrum shaping: QPSK with transparent FDSS-SE (ten sources) provides mostly -2 dB to 1 dB at SpEff 0.06–1.33, decreasing with SpEff; QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE (two sources) provides 1.4–2.6 dB (inner, single source) and 2.2–2.9 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.06–0.60, decreasing to -0.3 dB to 2.1 dB at SpEff 0.74–1.33; the non-transparent results are therefore higher, mainly at SpEff 0.06–0.60;
  *
Against QPSK with FDSS: QPSK with transparent FDSS-SE (seven sources) provides -2.0 dB to 2.8 dB (inner) and -1.9 dB to 1.8 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.38–1.4; QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides -0.2 dB to 1.0 dB at SpEff 0.38–0.60 (single source, outer only); the non-transparent result is therefore within the transparent range;
  *
Against QPSK with FDSS, with CFR applied to the reference scheme: only results for QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE were provided (-0.15 dB to 0.9 dB at SpEff 0.38–0.60, single source, outer only);
  *
Against QPSK with FDSS-SE: QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides only -0.1 dB to 0 dB at SpEff 0.23–0.74 and 0.1–0.2 dB at SpEff 0.88–1.18 (single source, outer only);
  *
Against QPSK without spectrum shaping, with CFR applied to the reference scheme: QPSK with transparent FDSS-SE provides -2.6 dB to 0.45 dB at SpEff 0.60–1.33 (two sources); QPSK with non-transparent FDSS-SE provides -0.3 dB to 1.45 dB at SpEff 0.74–1.33 (single source, outer only); both are therefore reduced, while the non-transparent upper end remains approximately 1 dB higher.

FDSS-ST: π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-ST generally shows higher reported gains than π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-ST, in particular against QPSK without spectrum shaping; however, against π/2-BPSK with FDSS, the outer non-transparent result is largely within the transparent range, and the non-transparent results rest on few and different sources.

  *
Against QPSK without spectrum shaping: π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-ST (six sources) provides -1.5 dB to 0.2 dB (inner) and -0.8 dB to 1.4 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.74–1.33; π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-ST (two sources) provides 1.9–2.6 dB (inner) at SpEff 0.74–0.88 and 0.9–2.0 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.75–1.31; the non-transparent results are therefore higher in this SpEff range;
  *
Against π/2-BPSK with FDSS: π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-ST (eleven sources) provides mostly -1.9 dB to 1.0 dB at SpEff 0.06–0.60, and -0.1 dB to 3.3 dB (inner) and -0.7 dB to 2.0 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.74–0.88; π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-ST provides 2.2–4.6 dB (inner, single source) at SpEff 0.19–0.88 and -1.8 dB to 1.2 dB (outer, single source) at SpEff 0.06–0.74; the inner non-transparent result is therefore higher, while the outer non-transparent result is largely within the transparent range;
  *
Against π/2-BPSK without spectrum shaping: only results for π/2-BPSK with non-transparent FDSS-ST were provided (0.7–1.6 dB at SpEff 0.06–0.38, decreasing to 0.1–1.2 dB at SpEff 0.49–0.88, single source);
  *
Against QPSK with FDSS: only results for π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-ST were provided (2.2–4.0 dB at SpEff 0.06–0.74 and -1.3 dB to 1.6 dB at SpEff 1.0–1.4, two sources, inner only);
  *
Against π/2-BPSK with FDSS or QPSK without spectrum shaping, with CFR applied to the reference scheme: only results for π/2-BPSK with transparent FDSS-ST were provided (against π/2-BPSK with FDSS: -2.1 dB to 0.6 dB (inner) and -1.7 dB to 0 dB (outer) at SpEff 0.06–0.60, single source; against QPSK without spectrum shaping: 0–1.0 dB at SpEff 0.60–0.88 and -1.9 dB to 0.6 dB at SpEff 1.03–1.33, two sources).

Regards,
Karri
[cid:88ee6a52-4d27-4f15-805e-c2a1e1029c7f]

From: 3gpp_tsg_ran_wg1: tsg ran working group 1 [log in to unmask]> on behalf of Karri Ranta-aho (Nokia) [log in to unmask]>
Sent: Monday, October 12, 2026 11:51
To: [log in to unmask] [log in to unmask]>
Subject: Re: [126bis-R20-6GR-Waveform]

Dear Waveform Colleagues,

Thank you for the excellent discussion on the offline.


  1.
Based on what we discussed, I have lifted a handful of FDSS observations from the summary that we could try to discuss online tonight. I have two alternative branches that we could pick which one to discuss, or even consider a merge.
  2.
I have another batch of observations on impact of filter change to FDSS. I have it here "just in case", to set the stage for potentially concluding that the 5G FDSS requirements that define the constraints of the filter could be revisited. We might not have the time to go there yet.
  3.
A proposal to update the RAN1#125 agreement on FDSS to remove the FFS point on QPSK and 16QAM. This would effectively limit the transparent FDSS to pi/2 BPSK
  4.
A proposed conclusion on the definition of what non-transparent means. We don't necessarily have to agree on this definition, the important point is to identify if this is broadly assumed by the group, or if there is controversy.

I will upload the FL summary#1 with a Tdoc number shortly.




Feature lead proposal:

Discuss the following observations alternatives on FDSS

Alternative 1

Transparent FDSS compared with no spectrum shaping (use cases 1–4): For π/2-BPSK (two sources), FDSS provides a net gain of 0.8–1.6 dB (outer) and -0.3 dB to 0.9 dB (inner) at SE 0.23–0.31. For QPSK (four sources), most results are within -2.8 dB to 0.9 dB at SE 0.23–1.33, with a large spread across sources. For 16QAM (two sources), FDSS results in a net loss of 2.2–3.6 dB (inner) and 1.5–2.9 dB (outer) at SE 1.48–2.57. When CFR is applied to the reference scheme, the net gain is -0.2 dB to 0.2 dB for QPSK at SE 0.74–1.33 (single source) and -0.7 dB to 0.2 dB for 16QAM at SE 1.33–2.57 (single source, inner only).

FDSS filter change (use cases 9 and 12, π/2-BPSK, outer RB allocation only): For transparent FDSS (three sources), the net gain is 0.1–4.6 dB at SE 0.06–0.60, with two sources reporting approximately 0 dB at SE 0.24, and -0.3 dB to 3.7 dB at SE 0.74. For non-transparent FDSS (three sources), two sources report a net gain of 0.6–0.9 dB and 2.5 dB at SE 0.06–0.60, while the third source reports 0–4.9 dB at SE 0.06–0.74, depending on the filter configuration. When CFR is applied to the reference scheme (single source), the net gain of non-transparent FDSS is 0.55–0.75 dB at SE 0.06–0.60.

Alternative 2

Compared with no spectrum shaping, transparent FDSS provides a net gain for π/2-BPSK, mainly for outer RB allocation. For QPSK, most results show a moderate net loss or a small net gain, with a large spread across sources. For 16QAM, most results show a net loss. When CFR is applied to the reference scheme, the net gain of FDSS for QPSK and 16QAM is within approximately ±0.7 dB.

-   FDSS for π/2-BPSK (Use case 1), reference scheme without CFR (two sources): a net gain of -0.3 dB to 0.9 dB (inner) and 0.8–1.6 dB (outer) at SE 0.23–0.31; one source reports a net gain of 3.6 dB at SE 0.54 (inner only). No results were provided with CFR applied to the reference scheme;

-   FDSS for QPSK (Use case 2), reference scheme without CFR (four sources): most results are within a net gain of -2.8 dB to 0.9 dB at SE 0.23–1.33, and outer RB allocation generally performs better than inner; one source reports net losses of up to 12.5 dB, and one source reports a net gain of 2.0 dB at SE 1.08 (inner only). With CFR applied to the reference scheme (single source), the net gain is -0.2 dB to -0.1 dB (inner) and 0.1–0.2 dB (outer) at SE 0.74–1.33;

-   FDSS for 16QAM (use case 3), reference scheme without CFR (two sources): a net loss of 2.2–3.6 dB (inner) and 1.5–2.9 dB (outer) at SE 1.48–2.57; one source reports a net gain of 0.2 dB at SE 2.16 (inner only). With CFR applied to the reference scheme (single source, inner only), the net gain is -0.7 dB to 0.2 dB at SE 1.33–2.57;


Discuss the following observations on FDSS with different filters

Comparing FDSS with a steeper filter, results available for π/2-BPSK  and outer RB allocations only.

-   Filter change for non-transparent FDSS for π/2-BPSK (Use case 9), reference scheme without CFR (three sources): a net gain of 0–4.9 dB at SE 0.06–0.74, decreasing slightly with increasing SE; the spread is mainly due to different filter configurations within one source, while the other sources report 0.6–0.9 dB and 2.5 dB at SE 0.06–0.60. With CFR applied to the reference scheme (single source), the net gain is 0.55–0.75 dB at SE 0.06–0.60;

-   Filter change for transparent FDSS for π/2-BPSK (Use case 12), reference scheme without CFR (three sources): a net gain of 0.1–4.6 dB at SE 0.06–0.60 and of -0.3 dB to 3.7 dB at SE 0.74; two sources report a net gain of approximately 0 dB at SE 0.24. No results were provided with CFR applied to the reference scheme.


Feature lead proposal:

Update the RAN1#125 agreement as follows:

  *   FDSS with transparent filtering should be supported in 6G is beneficial to be supported for π/2-BPSK from RAN1 perspective
     *   FFS: QPSK, 16QAM
  *   Draft LS to RAN4
     *   FFS: contents e.g., “the exact filter requirements are up to RAN4 discussions.”

Feature lead proposal:

Discuss the following conclusion:

  *   RAN1 work on non-transparent FDSS/FDSS-SE/FDSS-ST focuses on techniques where the DMRS and the data signal both go through the same filter. If a non-transparent FDSS/FDSS-SE/FDSS-ST is agreed to be included in 6G, the filter would be defined by RAN1.



Regards,
Karri

Dear all,

So far, we at least have 5 issues for evaluations

1)     RE pattern

2)     Phase continuity

3)     AOD vs. AOA

4)     Interference handling

5)     Beam related aspect (best Tx-Rx beam pair for sensing)

To accelerate the process, I draft a template for result collection. I use Yongqiang’s template as starting point. Removing some column, e.g., tracking related. Add some columns for the above 5 purpose.
/RAN/RAN1/Inbox/drafts/10.8 (ISAC)/10.8.2 (Aspects of integration)/Template of results collection

Till now, I just have one excel for all evaluations. I think it is easier to have the full pictures on the way to collect results in 10.8.2. later, we will have separate template for each simulation.
This document will NOT be discussed in tomorrow offline. Interested people please reach me for any comments. Thanks.

Best Regards
Yingyang

Dear all,

FL#1 has been uploaded as R1-2607824.

The following proposals and observations are going to be put forward in tomorrow morning’s online session.

Proposal 1-2-1 (A):
·        DCI-based dynamic activation is supported in 6GR for a SPS-PDSCH configuration.
·        DCI-based dynamic activation is at least supported in 6GR for a CG-PUSCH configuration which is not immediately activated upon the configuration.
·        FFS: Details of activation DCI for SPS-PDSCH configurations and CG-PUSCH configurations.
·        FFS: Application of activation DCI to a CG-PUSCH configuration which is immediately activated upon the configuration.
·        FFS: Potential application of sequence-based activation signaling, if a relevant need is identified.

Proposal 1-2-1 (B):
·        DCI-based dynamic activation is supported in 6GR for a SPS-PDSCH configuration.
·        DCI-based dynamic activation is at least supported in 6GR for a CG-PUSCH configuration which is not immediately activated upon the configuration.
·        FFS: Details of activation DCI for SPS-PDSCH configurations and CG-PUSCH configurations.
·        FFS: Application of activation DCI to a CG-PUSCH configuration which is immediately activated upon the configuration.
·        FFS: Potential application of sequence-based activation signaling, if a relevant need is identified.

Proposal 1-3-2: Support dynamic adjustment of parameters at least for SPS-PDSCH configurations and CG-PUSCH configurations that are not immediately activated and are subsequently activated by an activation DCI.

  *   FFS: Whether dynamic adjustment of parameters could also be applied to a CG-PUSCH configuration activated immediately upon the configuration.
     *   Note: If such support is agreed, a unified dynamic-adjustment DCI design should be pursued across all CG-PUSCH configurations and [SPS configurations].

Observation 1-3-1:

  *   NR already supports dynamic adjustment of parameters for SPS PDSCH and Type-2 CG PUSCH transmissions through activation (re-activation) DCI, demonstrating the benefits of adapting configured transmissions to varying traffic demands and channel conditions without RRC reconfiguration. [However, such adaptation is currently realized through re-activation procedures, which may introduce signaling overhead and procedural constraints in some scenarios.]
  *   Similar benefits may also be relevant for 6GR. Given the highly dynamic traffic characteristics, channel conditions, and spatial-domain environments anticipated for emerging services such as XR and AI traffic, dynamic adjustment of CG PUSCH and SPS PDSCH parameters could improve resource utilization, transmission efficiency, and adaptability to varying conditions[, while reducing the need for frequent RRC reconfiguration or repeated re-activation procedures].
  *   Note: The text enclosed with square brackets is subject to further discussion.

Proposal 2-1-1: From the RAN1 perspective, UL skipping is supported for CG-PUSCH in 6GR.

  *   For a UE configured with a CG-PUSCH configuration, the UE skips a CG-PUSCH transmission when no uplink payload is available for the CG-PUSCH.
     *   Further details are FFS.
·        Note: Further confirmation from RAN2 may be required regarding the support of UL skipping for CG-PUSCH.

Observation 2-1-2: UL skipping mechanism can enhance the efficiency of CG-PUSCH transmissions by avoiding unnecessary transmissions when no uplink data is available, leading to reduced UE power consumption and uplink interference.

Best regards,
Lei
